# The Middlegame: From Doctrine to a Real Package

## The gap this document exists to close

Be honest about what the folder contained before this document. The
conceptual chapters justify a worldview. The doctrine compresses it into
defaults. The field guide shows *positions* — snapshots of finished
packages with the pattern each one exhibits. The playbooks give *opening
theory* — the first eight moves for six recognizable situations. In chess
terms, the collection had openings, annotated positions, and endgame
tables, and was missing the genre that actually teaches judgment:
**annotated full games**, where you watch the decisions get made in
sequence, interacting, under pressure, with the alternatives visible and
the concessions priced.

The gap is structural, not editorial. Doctrine is stated per decision —
one principle, one rung, one encoding choice at a time — but a real
package is a *system of coupled decisions*: the presence policy constrains
the round-trip law, which constrains the open/closed choice, which feeds
back into what the validators may assume. Toy examples cannot exhibit
coupling, because coupling only appears when there are enough decisions to
couple. This is why the mature packages — ellmer, ragnar, quickr, rtemis —
feel categorically more complicated than anything in the playbooks: they
are not applying more patterns; they are absorbing the *interactions*.

So this document does two things. First it re-reads the mature four, not
for their patterns (the field guide's job) but for their **pressure
chains** — the sequence by which one hard requirement forced a cascade of
design consequences, including the concessions. Then it plays one
annotated game at realistic fidelity: a style-document core, derived
decision by decision, with the doctrine cited where it was followed and
overruled where reality outvoted it. The code for the load-bearing spine
was verified against S7 0.2.2 on R 4.6.1.

## Part I: How the mature four absorbed complexity

### ellmer: one requirement forces the hybrid

The instructive way to read ellmer is to ask what *forced* each piece of
its architecture, and the answer starts with a product requirement, not a
philosophy: **streaming**. A streamed response is a value that does not
exist yet — tokens accumulate over seconds, consumers want them as they
arrive, and the eventual `Turn` is only a fact once the stream closes.
Partial state must live *somewhere*, and no amount of value-semantics
conviction changes that. That single requirement makes the mutable `Chat`
object load-bearing: R6 is not a stylistic lapse but the honest home for
an accumulation-in-progress, and the doctrine's actual contribution is
*containment* — completed turns crystallize into immutable S7 values, the
conversation is reconstructible from the values alone, and the mutable rim
stays one class wide.

The second chain: **provider variation**. Every supported provider has
quirks — capabilities, wire formats, authentication, streaming protocols —
and the `Provider` dispatch surface absorbs them. The price, visible if
you watch the package evolve, is that a plugin surface *grows*: each new
provider capability becomes a new generic or a new argument somewhere, and
the interface can never again be reorganized cheaply because third parties
stand on it. The lesson for the middlegame: doctrine 10 tells you to
design the verb vocabulary carefully; ellmer shows *why the stakes are
asymmetric* — under-designing an internal function costs a refactor,
under-designing an extension surface costs an ecosystem migration.

### ragnar: the price tag on base-type inheritance

The compendium praises `MarkdownDocumentChunks` inheriting from tibble as
"honest base-type inheritance" — the value really is a table. The
middlegame reading adds the invoice: **inheriting a base type means the
parent's entire API becomes your unvalidated mutator set.** Every dplyr
verb, every `[` method, every tool in the tibble ecosystem can transform
the object along paths where the subclass's laws are never consulted —
drop the columns the class depends on, break the alignment with
`@document`, or silently strip the subclass entirely. ragnar's concession
is that its invariants on that surface are documented rather than
enforced, and re-established at the operations that matter. That is a
rational trade — the whole point of inheriting tibble is to *get* that
ecosystem — but it is a trade, and the doctrine's "construction is the
proof" holds only on the package's own front doors, not on the thousand
side doors the parent class ships with. When you inherit a base type, you
are choosing which of those doors to guard, and accepting the rest.

### quickr: power through refusal

quickr compiles R to Fortran, and the design decision that makes it
possible is what it *declines*: it accepts a subset of R, requires
`declare(type())` annotations, and errors on constructs it cannot compile
faithfully rather than approximating their semantics. This is doctrine 17
— refuse to guess — applied not to an argument default but to the entire
domain of the tool: **shrink the promise until you can keep it.** The
middlegame lesson generalizes to every "model an existing thing" project:
the fastest route to a robust core is usually not handling more of the
input space, it is drawing a smaller boundary you can defend completely,
with loud errors at the fence. Coverage grows later, fence post by fence
post, each one tested. The packages that tried to accept everything on
day one are the ones whose validators are full of guesses.

### rtemis: the fixed cost of constraints-as-data

rtemis's property-factory stratum — the `PropertySpec` machinery deriving
validators, defaults, JSON Schema, and TUI forms from single declarations
— is the compendium's favorite exhibit for constraints-as-data. The
middlegame reading prices it: that stratum is itself a serious system,
hundreds of lines of meta-machinery that every contributor must understand
before they can add a property, and every error message now has an extra
layer of indirection between the symptom and the declaration. It
amortizes because rtemis has *hundreds* of hyperparameters across dozens
of models and genuinely needs all four projections. Below some scale
threshold — and most packages are below it — hand-written
`new_property()` calls are not a failure to apply the pattern; they are
the pattern correctly not applied (doctrine 15: the third occurrence, not
the first). The factory stratum is the right move exactly when you can
name the projections you need and count the declarations that will pay
for it.

### The shared shape

Four packages, one shape: each met a pressure that made the naive,
doctrine-by-the-letter design uneconomic — streaming broke pure values,
ecosystem reuse broke enforced invariants, R's full semantics broke
compilability, hyperparameter count broke hand-written validation. And
each responded the same way: **not by abandoning a principle but by
moving where it applies** — containing state instead of forbidding it,
guarding chosen doors instead of all doors, shrinking the promise instead
of diluting it, buying machinery only where the census showed volume.
That move — relocating a principle's jurisdiction instead of revoking it
— is the core middlegame skill, and it is exactly what per-decision
doctrine cannot teach and an annotated game can.

## Part II: An annotated game

The domain: a core for map-style documents — the root, its sources, its
layers, their paint. Chosen because it is real, the spec pressure is
genuine (hundreds of paint properties, embedded expressions, ongoing spec
evolution), and it exercises three playbooks at once (spec modeling,
embedded language, and the temptation of a stateful manager). What
follows is a derivation, not project work: ten decisions in dependency
order, each with its pressure, its options, and its resolution — doctrine
cited when followed, named when overruled.

### Move 1: Scope — model what your operations touch

The census (playbook 1, move 2) says the spec is far too large to model
at once: root, sources, layers, sprite, glyphs, terrain, fog, transitions,
and a paint vocabulary in the hundreds. The pressure is real and the
answer is an ordering, not an ambition: model the nodes your *operations*
touch — construction, mutation, serialization of root/sources/layers —
and let everything else pass through as inert wire data until an
operation needs it. Deferral is not debt if the pass-through is lossless;
it is the vertical-slice discipline applied to scope.

### Move 2: Rung 0 — the engine's validator, and gold files

The engine ships an authoritative validator; re-implementing it in R
would be expression-system envy at document scale. Rung 0 is: gold files
produced by reference tooling, round-trip tests against them, and the
engine validator run in CI where a JS runtime is available. Every
subsequent decision about what *we* validate assumes this floor exists.

### Move 3: The layer family — three principles collide

The pivotal decision of the whole game. Layers come in a dozen types
(fill, line, symbol, raster, ...) that differ in behavior and in their
paint vocabularies — doctrine 8 says subclass family, and dispatch
genuinely wants it (validation, legend generation, rendering hints all
vary by type). But each type's paint vocabulary is dozens of properties,
churned by spec releases — hand-modeling four hundred paint properties as
S7 properties is schema cosplay by volume, and doctrine 16 says generate
tables, not class graphs. Meanwhile the paint values themselves can be
literals *or* expressions, which doctrine 8 would encode as a union.

The resolution is a **two-level hybrid, with the split placed exactly at
the dispatch boundary**: layer *types* become subclasses, because
behavior dispatches on them; paint becomes a *validated bag* — one list
property, checked against a generated spec table. The bag is a
denormalization doctrine 8 would frown at, chosen consciously: variant
honesty is paid for where dispatch collects the benefit (the type level)
and declined where it would cost four hundred properties tracking a
moving spec (the paint level). The spec table is constraints-as-data —
rtemis's pattern at the scale where it actually amortizes:

```r
# generated from the engine's style-spec json, one row per paint property;
# excerpt shown - the real table is machine-derived, never hand-edited
paint_spec <- list(
  fill = list(
    `fill-color`   = list(type = "color"),
    `fill-opacity` = list(type = "number", minimum = 0, maximum = 1)
  ),
  line = list(
    `line-color` = list(type = "color"),
    `line-width` = list(type = "number", minimum = 0)
  )
)

check_paint <- function(paint, type) {
  spec <- paint_spec[[type]]
  bad <- character()
  for (nm in names(paint)) {
    rule <- spec[[nm]]
    if (is.null(rule)) {
      bad <- c(bad, paste0("unknown paint property '", nm, "'"))
      next
    }
    val <- paint[[nm]]
    if (is_expression(val)) next   # move 4: rung 1, the engine judges these
    if (identical(rule$type, "number") && is.numeric(val)) {
      if (!is.null(rule$minimum) && val < rule$minimum) {
        bad <- c(bad, paste0("'", nm, "' below minimum ", rule$minimum))
      }
      if (!is.null(rule$maximum) && val > rule$maximum) {
        bad <- c(bad, paste0("'", nm, "' above maximum ", rule$maximum))
      }
    }
  }
  if (length(bad)) bad
}
```

Note what the interaction did: doctrine 16 (generate tables) is what made
overruling doctrine 8 (honest variants) *safe* — the bag is lawless only
as a class shape; the table restores the laws at validation time, and the
same table can later project documentation or a paint-builder UI (the
reverse arrow of [06-documents-schemas-dsls.qmd](06-documents-schemas-dsls.qmd)).
Neither principle alone produces this design; their collision does.

### Move 4: Expressions — rung 1, stated as a policy not an omission

Paint values may be expressions (`["interpolate", ["zoom"], ...]`). The
escalation ladder says opaque passthrough until analysis is the product,
so `check_paint()` contains one line — `if (is_expression(val)) next` —
and that line *is* the policy: expressions are the engine's jurisdiction.
The trap this dodges is the validator slowly learning the expression
grammar, one special case at a time, until it is a bad reimplementation
of the engine (expression-system envy). The upgrade path is already
written down: if legend generation ever becomes a requirement, that is
the `fields_used()` justification test from
[09-playbooks.qmd](09-playbooks.qmd), and the climb goes to combinators,
not directly to an AST.

### Move 5: The layer classes — thin, because the table is thick

```r
layer <- S7::new_class("layer", abstract = TRUE, properties = list(
  id     = S7::class_character,
  source = S7::class_character,
  paint  = S7::new_property(S7::class_list, default = list())
))

fill_layer <- S7::new_class("fill_layer", parent = layer,
  validator = function(self) check_paint(self@paint, "fill")
)
line_layer <- S7::new_class("line_layer", parent = layer,
  validator = function(self) check_paint(self@paint, "line")
)
```

Each subclass validator is one delegation line. This is the checking
ladder holding under load: type lives on the property classes, paint law
lives in the table, and the subclass's only job is to bind its type tag
to the table lookup. A dozen layer types cost a dozen three-line classes
— which is also the honest test that the move-3 hybrid was right: had we
hand-modeled paint, each of these classes would be a hundred lines of
property declarations chasing the spec.

### Move 6: Presence and the round-trip law — decided together, or wrong

Paint properties have engine-defined defaults (`fill-opacity` defaults to
1 in the engine). The presence decision: **do not store engine defaults.**
An omitted key means "engine default," and the model preserves the
distinction between *omitted* and *explicitly set to the default value* —
because a user who wrote `fill-opacity: 1` and a user who wrote nothing
have expressed different things, and a future spec release could change
the default out from under the silent one. This immediately constrains
the round-trip law (the equality taxonomy of
[06-documents-schemas-dsls.qmd](06-documents-schemas-dsls.qmd)): the
promise is *canonical equality* on modeled fields and *representational
preservation* on the paint bag — not wire equivalence, precisely because
wire equivalence would license resolving defaults, which is the one
normalization this design forbids. Two decisions, one lock: neither the
presence policy nor the equality relation could have been chosen alone.

### Move 7: The root, and the laws only it can see

```r
style <- S7::new_class("style", properties = list(
  sources = S7::new_property(S7::class_list, default = list()),
  layers  = S7::new_property(S7::class_list, default = list())
), validator = function(self) {
  ids  <- vapply(self@layers, function(l) l@id, character(1))
  refs <- vapply(self@layers, function(l) l@source, character(1))
  msgs <- character()
  if (anyDuplicated(ids)) msgs <- c(msgs, "layer ids must be unique")
  missing_refs <- setdiff(refs, names(self@sources))
  if (length(missing_refs)) {
    msgs <- c(msgs, paste("layer references unknown source:", missing_refs))
  }
  if (length(msgs)) msgs
})
```

Id uniqueness and source resolution are laws no layer can check — they
mention the collection. The aggregate-root rung earns its place here, and
note the granularity call (an open question the ledger tracks): this
design has *one* root despite the document's depth, because both
cross-object laws happen to be visible from the top. A spec with
cross-references three levels down would force the nested-root question
this game gets to skip.

### Move 8: Mutators — the front door, with preconditions

```r
add_layer <- function(style, layer, before = NULL) {
  layers <- style@layers
  if (!is.null(before)) {
    ids <- vapply(layers, function(l) l@id, character(1))
    pos <- match(before, ids)
    if (is.na(pos)) {
      cli::cli_abort("no layer with id {.val {before}} to insert before.")
    }
    layers <- append(layers, list(layer), after = pos - 1)
  } else {
    layers <- c(layers, list(layer))
  }
  S7::set_props(style, layers = layers)
}
```

`before` not existing is an *operation* error (rung: method
precondition), distinct from the structural laws below it — the message
can therefore speak the operation's language ("insert before"), which no
class validator could. And a verified interaction worth knowing:
`set_props()` re-runs the root validator, so a duplicate id introduced
*through the mutator* is rejected by the root's law without the mutator
checking it — the rungs genuinely do not duplicate each other, and the
insertion order, precondition failure, and duplicate rejection were all
confirmed live.

### Move 9: Ids — the tier-1 answer to the atoms-versus-earning tension

Should `layer_id` be a semantic type? It is a meaning, not just a string
— doctrine 1 wants it named early; doctrine 15 wants abstraction earned.
The concrete resolution uses the tiers: a *reused property definition*
(tier 1 — one `new_property()` value shared by every id-shaped slot)
names the meaning and centralizes its law at near-zero cost, while a
full class (tier 2/3) waits until something dispatches on ids or ids
grow structure. The tension between two principles, unresolvable in the
abstract, costs one line to resolve in the concrete — which is itself a
middlegame lesson: many doctrinal collisions are cheap at the point of
decision and only look profound in prose.

### Move 10: The manager that must not exist

Every document model eventually tempts its author with a `StyleManager`
R6 class — "convenient" mutable state holding the current style, an undo
stack, a dirty flag. The fact/process sort (playbook 5) says no: a style
is a fact through and through; reading, patching, and writing it are
shell *functions*; and an undo stack, if wanted, is a list of immutable
snapshots — which value semantics makes nearly free (structural sharing:
the copies share every untouched payload, per the verified probes in
[02-values-and-state.qmd](02-values-and-state.qmd)). The mutable manager
would buy nothing and sell local reasoning. Declined, by name, on the
record.

### The game's concessions, tallied

An annotated game ends by admitting what it conceded, because the
concessions are where the doctrine's edges live:

- **The paint bag is a flattened product** (overrules the letter of
  doctrine 8), made safe by the generated table (doctrine 16) — the
  overrule and its mitigation are one decision, not two.
- **Unknown paint keys are currently rejected** (closed node), which is
  the strict choice; a package prioritizing round-trip fidelity for
  foreign styles would flip this to a pass-through with the table
  checking only known keys. The choice is defensible either way; making
  it *by accident* is not. This one is flagged for revisit.
- **The spec table is trusted, not verified** — its correctness is
  inherited from the generation pipeline against the engine's spec JSON,
  which quietly relocates rung 0 upstream. A stale table is now the
  design's single most dangerous failure mode, which is exactly the
  single-source-of-truth trade: one datum, one point of failure.
- **What the toy still hides:** the real table generation pipeline, the
  sprite and glyph subsystems, wire-version migration, and every print
  method, error message, and documentation page — the unglamorous
  majority of a real package that no design document shortens much.

## Part III: The loop that actually transfers the wisdom

The last honest thing this document can say is that no document — not
this one — converts wisdom into skill. The mature four were not designed
by consulting a compendium; they were designed by people making
decisions, hitting walls, and revising. What a compendium can do is
shorten that loop: make the decision points visible sooner, the options
nameable, and the concessions explicit instead of accidental. The
transfer mechanism is a practice, and it is cheap:

**Keep a design journal in the project.** One entry per real decision,
five lines: the decision, the pressure, the options considered, the
choice, and the principle followed *or overruled, with the reason*. The
annotated game above is exactly this journal, written after the fact;
writing it during the fact is faster and truer. The journal does two
jobs at once: it makes "selectively considering the proper aspects" an
explicit act instead of an anxiety (you consulted the doctrine, you cited
or overruled it, done — no lingering doubt about whether you *should*
have used some sophisticated pattern you decided against), and it
produces the evidence stream the compendium needs to stay alive — a
recurring overrule in your journals is a counterexample entry for
[open-questions.qmd](open-questions.qmd), and a pattern that keeps earning
across your projects is a promotion candidate.

**Review the journal at complexity checkpoints, not on a schedule.** The
natural checkpoints: the first mutator (is the invariant placement
holding?), the first serializer (did presence and equality get decided
together?), the tenth class (is a factory stratum starting to amortize?),
the first external implementor (is the interface really a contract?).
These are the moments the middlegame pressure chains start, and a
half-hour against the doctrine's decision guides at each one is worth
more than any amount of up-front design piety.

That is the whole method: openings from the playbooks, this document's
annotated game as the model for the middlegame, the journal as your own
annotation habit, and the ledger as the place your games feed back into
the theory. Eating our own food is not a property the compendium can
have by itself — it is a loop the compendium and the projects run
together.
